[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements!

Orwell takes an interesting premise and turns the investigatory gameplay into clicking and dragging blue-underlined phrases into a database, or navigating conflicting yellow-underlined “choices.” The music adds some weight to the situation, the story escalates well, and there are real consequences to your actions. While it becomes a little over the top, that is to be expected in a video game. Overall, it was an interesting experience—especially when thinking about the modern surveillance systems we have today, such as databases and Flock cameras.

It really made me think about privacy concerns, and how individuals will sacrifice personal freedoms in order to exist in a society. However, there are often bad actors who will use those restrictions to push their own beliefs, frequently using phrases like “children’s safety” while actively restricting freedoms. I still think about the stories surrounding Flock cameras where police officers looked up their ex-girlfriends' locations at different times; if you Google the story, you can find several variations of this happening with guys in San Jose, Kentucky, and Texas.

I am not against the idea of being able to go through people’s information when searching for a crime, but there need to be heavy safeguards, or individuals' privacy and freedoms will always be invalidated. This raises the question of who makes those choices, and what is considered a valid reason to override a person’s individual freedoms. The fact of the matter is, I don’t think our society could ever be built on the idea of simultaneously respecting individual freedoms and maintaining public order; however, I still cannot advocate for an organization's ability to rifle through a person’s private information. That being said, it was certainly fun to do so in a video game. While there are some things that could have been improved and I would have liked a bit more content, the game was meant to be a short, contained experience, and it does that job well.

For a game of mostly dialogue, the writing is pretty bad. Dialogues are full of cliches, characters are incredibly unlikeable, especially the first character you investigate who is just a narcissistic turd. If anything, the game makes a compelling argument FOR a nanny state, because these people all suck. I also have no clue why you have a handler, as all they do is say the most inane, mindless, stupid things whenever you upload a clue. Upload a person's interest in hiking and "Oh, she likes to go outside. Interesting." It's like the most boring person in the world is looking over your shoulder watching you work and commenting. 

The gameplay is also pretty deceptive. It makes it seem like you can omit information and be subversive, but some information is required to move forward, and you don't know which until the game just stops moving forward. So if you wanted to make someone seem like they aren't a terrorist or are, you can't. Which felt like the whole point of the game? A lot of decisions, like choosing which person's photo is on their dossier, are entirely irrelevant. It's just padding to make it seem like you are doing more than you are. In fact, most of the choices you make aren't choices. The ending also gets to the exact same climax regardless.

Also a weird decision to highlight the relevant sections to upload. I was essentially just skimming every document for the highlighted bit and going 'okay, that's the part that matters' and ignoring the rest. I say this as a person that likes to read, but because it hand holds you, you just click on the tab it tells you to click (with a helpful red exclamation mark) then click the text it tells you to click, and if there ever IS a decision, like two conflicting pieces of information that might make someone seem bad, it helpfully tells you not to make a mistake and wait until you get more info to submit that info, basically cutting out the only agency you might have as a player.

Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

[h1] Orwell: The Government’s Digital "Nosy Neighbor" Simulator [/h1]

Have you ever wanted to snoop on someone else’s text messages and dig through their browser history to sniff out their secrets, while getting paid by the state to do it? Welcome to Orwell.

[h2] The Plot: Big Brother is Watching (Except Big Brother is YOU) [/h2]
The capital has just been bombed. Instead of sending out tactical agents with guns like in an action movie, the government hands you a top-secret software called Orwell.

Your mission? Sit back comfortably behind a computer screen, scouring every corner of social media, private chats, bank accounts, and even dating profiles of the suspects. In short, you're a cyber investigator with the power and nosiness of a super-level neighbor: you know all the town's drama.

The gameplay is super chill: read, scroll to find info, and drag-and-drop it into the database. But the funniest (and most wicked) part of the game lies in context.
You work under a boss named Symes. The catch is that this boss is completely clueless about the raw data you're reading; he only sees what you choose to report. Real-world example:
[olist]
    [*]A guy posts a status: "Oh god I'm losing my mind, I want to blow up this city!" because he just dropped his fully loaded boba tea.
    [*]You crop just the sentence "I want to blow up this city" and send it up to the system.
    [*]Congratulations, the boba enthusiast is instantly labeled a terrorist, and SWAT is kicking down his door in the next 5 minutes.
[/olist]
And that's the game's highlight, its terrifying relevance: Long before modern debates about data collection, AI surveillance, and privacy became as prevalent as they are today, Orwell grasped just how easily personal data could be weaponized.

Not to mention the game's interface makes you look like a cool Hollywood hacker saving the world, even though you're just browsing the internet and reading comments.

But after all, if you don't like reading text logs, chat transcripts, and fictional articles, the gameplay loop can feel like doing administrative homework.

The idea is excellent: You're an operative tasked with monitoring the social media and activities of various individuals suspected of or likely to carry out terrorist attacks, with the goal of stopping them. Initially, everything seems quite obvious and trivial, but it soon begins to explore gray areas and presents very interesting moral dilemmas.

After playing through it a couple of times, you become aware of the intricate plot and how linear it is, but during your first playthrough, it's practically imperceptible. It manages to create a strong sense of decision-making and truly draw you into its narrative. You genuinely feel like a spy because perhaps that's exactly what your job would look like if you were one. You would stop seeing people as individuals and begin to see them as pixels. That's the magic of Orwell.

The only important point to note is that it's heavily dependent on the language you speak. If the game isn't in a language you're fluent in, I recommend not playing it, as the game demands a lot from you in interpreting very specific data and dialogue, which could cause you to miss some excellent details that enhance the experience.

First of all it's not detective work, you just drop pieces of information in a database hoping it makes the story progress.

Because you're not technically forced to drop all the information in the database, you quickly try to have an impact on the story's progression by keeping some info to yourself, but the story only progresses when specific info is used and you never know which info is necessary or not so you can't really make informed choices on what to give Orwell and what to not.

I quickly find myself stuck with the story not progressing because I've decided to keep a piece of information that's mandatory for the story to continue and so I have to start from the top and review everything which is tedious and drop random bits of information I've kept until I find the one that was necessary for the story to continue which means I really can't choose what I keep or don't keep,

or I straight up give all the info away from the start to not have to review everything later once I'm stuck which again means I can't choose what I keep or don't keep.

There seems to be a system of highlighting the files where there still is relevant information but I don't understand how it works. Sometimes files are highlighted and there's nothing left on them and sometimes they aren't highlighted and there's still important things on them. It's very confusing.

I also suspect the political messaging of the game is really not so subtle and just "violence is bad" with no nuance but I can't tell you for sure because I'm too frustrated with the gameplay to go to the end of the story at this point. My other issue with the writing that I just can't seem to get over is that it makes zero sense that people who are fighting surveillance would post on the internet about it with their full name and photo or extremely basic aliases. Not posting about your actions on the internet is activism 101.

Okay-ish. I feel like core mechanics are not utilized enough and there is room for making gameplay more enjoyable. I guess this is because you're limited in options a bit too much, but I can't remember for sure.

This game really does sell the vibe that you're an analyst working inside of Orwell's system, while never feeling tedious or contrived, a big achievement in my book. But of course, the real pull of a game like this is its ability to explore difficult themes about freedom of expression, security, surveillance, checks and balances, etc...

I found the narrative compelling and nuanced. The gameplay effectively branches narratives based on the prejudices of the player and it was interesting to see how an individual with different philosophies might simply follow a different rabbit hole, never stumbling upon the same "truths" that I had. In presenting the narrative this way, the creators wrote a fair bit of nuance into the story: little arcs that can be easily missed if someone's inclined one way or another on a controversial subject. The tension between the themes is reasonably well managed and the endings express different morals; I find the decision to not conclusively state a moral position to be quite brave from the creators' parts and such a decision serves the broader concept of the game very well. 

In considering games as art, I think Orwell provides an excellent example of an expression that is best explored through the medium of video games. Orwell feels like a fledgling OS, simple, sleek, intuitive as an Apple product, creepy and intrusive as a Google one. As a user, you are complicit in the structures of surveillance and, while you have some authority on how to navigate the complex moral questions in front of you (and in doing so, revealing your own biases), there is a palpable sense that this apparatus is large, amorphous, and exuding a sense of clinical evil that only exists with oppressive regimes or corporations. In other words, this game conveys appropriately both the individual and systemic realities of mass surveillance. Now onto my main gripe.

The characters are all viciously annoying human beings. While I certainly understand that in order to create a game with significant nuance in the face of large, controversial themes, individual characters almost necessarily have to retain both positive and negative qualities (a very human characterization), I nevertheless ended up finding the characters insufferable. If my ID had its way, these asshats would all be jailed simply for being pompous, room-temperature IQ, morons with the total and absolute inability to make a single correct decision in their lives. Even characters I initially found likeable or at least, found myself agreeing with, ended up talking their way into these childish and absurd holes and given that the characters are crucial to the gameplay and their interactions are the basis for plot advancement, I often found reading their texts quite a drag. 

Overall, a solid exploration of difficult themes through a very effective medium. Props to the creators for their creativity, narrative complexity, and willingness to engage with controversial subjects without tribalism or devolving into virtue-signaling. I especially like how the game exposes your own biases (though never in an explicit manner). May Hancock slowly rot into agonizing, ego-shattering insanity as he's thrown into the darkest dungeon.
